chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said: 'When does food become prohibited for the fasting person, and when does the Fajr prayer become permissible?' He said to me, 'When dawn appears and is like the white sheet (al-qubtiyyah al-bayda'), then food becomes prohibited and the Fajr prayer becomes permissible.' I said: 'So we are not in the time [of prohibition] until the ray of the sun rises?' He said, 'Far off! Where are you going? That is the prayer of the children.'

key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: Dawn, specifically the time for Fajr prayer and the start of fasting
key_terms.الْقُبْطِيَّةِ الْبَيْضَاءِ: The white sheet, a specific visual sign of dawn indicating the start of fasting
key_terms.شُعَاعُ الشَّمْسِ: The ray of the sun, the time of actual sunrise
key_terms.صَلَاةُ الصِّبْيَانِ: The prayer of the children, referring to the earlier, less precise time of dawn used by those who are not careful

ai.seo_question: When does the prohibition of eating begin during the day of fasting according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between *al-fajr al-sadiq* (true dawn) and *al-fajr al-kadhib* (false dawn), establishing the former as the legal cutoff for fasting. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) corrects the common misconception of waiting for sunrise by emphasizing that the prohibition begins with the horizontal spread of light, while the 'prayer of the children' refers to the earlier, less precise time used for voluntary prayers or by those not strictly observing the fast's boundaries. This distinction is foundational in Shia fiqh for determining the exact start of the daily fast.
